statement: Among the same 12 healthy volunteers with hallucinogen experience who took part in a series of laboratory sessions with placebo, triazolam and rising single doses of dextromethorphan (DXM), about one month after the last session no one reported lasting distress or lasting changes in perception, and no one had called the study team about problems after a session, although one person chose not to take a dose again and reported a headache after that session. On a questionnaire about lasting changes, participants reported positive changes in attitudes, mood, relationships, behaviour and spirituality (46% to 61% of maximum scores, with low negative ratings) and all 12 said their well-being had increased; 4 of 12 rated the sessions among the five most meaningful experiences of their lives. The questionnaire covered all sessions together and could not separate DXM sessions from triazolam or placebo sessions; participants knew the laboratory's psilocybin research, were carefully prepared and supported, and people with a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar illness were excluded, so these reports may not apply to unsupervised use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: About a month after their last laboratory session, none of the twelve volunteers reported lasting upset or lasting changes in what they saw or heard, and most said the sessions had changed them for the better. But the questions covered all their sessions together, including dummy-pill and sleeping-pill days, the volunteers expected meaningful experiences and were well looked after, and people at higher risk of psychosis were not allowed to take part.
population: Healthy adults aged 20 to 40 (9 men, 3 women) with LSD and psilocybin experience, without substance dependence and without personal or family psychotic or bipolar illness
exposure: A series of supervised laboratory sessions with placebo, triazolam and rising single doses of dextromethorphan (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: None for the one-month reports (the questionnaire did not separate sessions)
outcome: Self-reported persisting effects (143-item questionnaire), personal meaning, spiritual significance and well-being at about one month; reports of distress or perceptual changes after sessions
magnitude: Positive persisting-effect scales 46% to 61% of maximum, negative ratings low; 4 of 12 'among the 5 most meaningful experiences', 7 of 12 'among the 5 most spiritually significant'; well-being increased in all 12 (1 slightly, 7 moderately, 4 very much); 0 of 12 reported lasting distress or persisting perceptual phenomena; 1 of 12 stopped after a post-session headache.

evidence.page: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire
evidence.locator: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: About one month after the final session: positive changes in attitudes about life and self, mood, social effects, behaviour and spirituality at 46% to 61% of maximum scores, negative ratings low; 4 of 12 rated the experiences among the five most meaningful of their lives and 7 of 12 among the five most spiritually significant; all 12 reported increased well-being (1 slightly, 7 moderately, 4 very much). The questionnaire could not separate DXM from triazolam sessions; in interviews, effects were attributed to sessions thought to be a classic hallucinogen.

One participant reached a stop point by declining that dose again and reported a post-session headache attributed to DXM; the primary monitor was reachable by phone throughout, no volunteer called or reported distress after the sessions, and no lasting distress or persisting perceptual phenomena were reported at the one-month follow-up.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors note that volunteers knew the laboratory's psilocybin research and may have expected psilocybin, and that preparation, social support and the setting may have shaped their positive ratings; people with a personal or immediate-family history of schizophrenia, bipolar, delusional, paranoid or schizoaffective disorder were excluded.

risk_of_bias.note: Self-reported, unblinded follow-up covering all sessions; expectancy and setting effects acknowledged by the authors.

indirectness.note: Worded for screened volunteers in supervised sessions; people at higher psychiatric risk excluded.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive self-reports without a comparison start low. Risk of bias -1 (self-report after supportive sessions, expectancy, no separation of drug conditions). Imprecision -1 (12 people). Very low. Single study.
